meta.title: The AI Crash Is Over. Here's What Comes Next
meta.thread_line: 5 threads · speed-crash bottom call, new hedging framework, Gavin Baker on compute scarcity, hyperscaler/Google/memory cracks, Fed-yen intervention and debasement trade

snapshot: Visser declares the 2026 AI "speed crash" over — bottom is in "as far as I'm concerned on a probability basis"; a ~10% 4-day rally on the Nasdaq-100 was the strongest move of its kind in 17 years (since the GFC), with 80%+ of his 100-name AI thematic portfolio back above a rising 200-day moving average.

This week's tape: S&P +3.6%, Nasdaq-100 +5%, his AI thematic portfolio +6.5% (2nd-best week of the year); YTD S&P +13% with every sector positive, and new all-time highs across IWM, the NYSE Composite, equal-weight S&P, the DAX, and the FTSE.

Volatility and credit have normalized fast: VIX at January lows, single-name equity vol back to pre-panic levels, CDX credit index showing no stress — a direct rebuttal to traders who bought S&P puts expecting contagion.

Most of the video is a new hedging framework for what Visser calls a "structurally different" market, because AI is "compressing economic time": built on his own 100-name diversified AI index (no standard benchmark exists), factor volatility instead of index (VIX) volatility, and a 50-day rate-of-change signal that already flagged the July top and got him out of Micron in time.

He calls Gavin Baker's recent interview a "must listen regardless of your views on AI" — Baker argues there's zero evidence of decelerating demand and hyperscalers are in "acute compute shortage," with GPU rental pricing actually rising (a B200 cluster went from ~$2/hr to near $4/GPU-hour in seven months).

Two structural risks flagged for later this decade: hyperscaler free cash flow staying negative for years per Goldman Sachs despite heavy capex, and the memory supply/demand imbalance Elon Musk confirmed on SpaceX's earnings call (supply +20%/yr vs. demand +200%/yr) as a bottleneck independent of GPU compute.

Also covered: the first coordinated US-Japan FX intervention since 1998 to prop up the yen (and indirectly the Treasury market), still-elevated odds (45%) of a September Fed hike despite Kevin Warsh giving no guidance, and a strong debasement-trade week for gold (+7.2%, third-best in 16 years), silver, and platinum.

themes.status: BOTTOM CALLED — ON A PROBABILITY BASIS
themes.title: The AI "Speed Crash" Is Over, Bottom Is In
themes.lead: Visser's headline call: the historic volatility event is behind us, and the rally off the bottom has the hallmarks of a real low, not a bear-market bounce.
bullets: The rally off the low got close to 10% on the Nasdaq-100 over four trading days — the biggest move of its kind in 17 years since the Great Financial Crisis, alongside famous bottoms like Liberation Day and COVID.

Key difference from a typical bear-market rally: the S&P and 80%+ of his AI thematic names held above a 200-day moving average that is still pointed upward — his long-standing rule for what separates a real bull market from a bounce.

S&P 4-day rate of change hit 6%, the biggest in the past year; the rally was 6 percentage points bigger than the entire 3-month "pennant flag" range (May-July) it broke out of — "that is not something to fade."

Week's tape: S&P +3.6%, Nasdaq-100 +5%, his AI thematic portfolio +6.5% (2nd-biggest week of the year); YTD S&P +13% with every sector green, new all-time highs in IWM, the NYSE Composite, equal-weight S&P, the DAX, and the FTSE; South Korea's KOSPI +61% YTD with its tech sector +116%.

Volatility and credit confirm the "cleansing event" thesis: factor volatility and single-name vol have both collapsed back toward pre-panic levels (evidence funds de-grossed or hedged), VIX is at January lows, and the CDX credit index shows no stress — traders who bought S&P puts expecting contagion "lost on the direction" and "lost on the vol."

Earnings backdrop supporting the bounce: EPS growth near 50%, revenue growth ~15% since Q1 2025, margins up from 13% to 17% year-over-year, breadth at its best level since July 14 with the 200-day slope 80%+ pointed upward, and PMI plus non-defense-ex-air durable goods both approaching 60.

quote.text: The bottom is in as far as I'm concerned on a probability basis. If we take out the lows, I'd be surprised.

themes.watch: This is a probability call, not a certainty — Visser says explicitly "you never know," and notes that several market commentators he's been listening to remain bearish into the rally, positioned for a false breakout.

themes.title: Hedging AI: Why Index Puts Stopped Working
themes.lead: Visser's central practical message this week: the market is structurally different now, so hedge with factor volatility and his own diversified index, not standard index options.
bullets: Core thesis: AI is "compressing economic time," which he argues makes this bull market permanently different — terminal values get harder to estimate, and stocks can swing from a 30x to a 20x P/E "in a very short amount of time" (he cites Google as a current example).

Gross leverage is at all-time highs — he calls this "peak gross leverage" and expects factor volatility to stay structurally higher (settling around 25-30 rather than returning to pre-crash lows) as leverage normalizes over the next few years.
Because factor volatility (an equal-weighted blend of momentum, value, quality, and beta) has broken away from index volatility, "using index puts is not going to work the way that it used to."

His replacement is a price-and-time framework: a 50-day rate-of-change reading on his 100-name AI thematic portfolio. A ~50% move over 50 trading days (about two months) is a hard warning sign; risk starts building once that reading passes 20%.

This signal already worked in practice — it flagged the top before the index itself peaked, and it's what led him to sell all of his Micron in July and rotate into silver, Bitcoin, and Eli Lilly, all of which he says outperformed through the subsequent drawdown.

New tool released this week: an "earnings mosaic" prompt (run in ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Grok) that combines his technical sheet with that week's earnings commentary — demoed on Eaton and Schneider Electric, both electrical-infrastructure names that reported this week and are both Vera Rubin ecosystem participants.

Names he flags as not yet bounced but still held: Palantir ("the only software name I own personally," which he says the shorts "are missing something" on), Fluence, and two more heard on auto-captions as "Comores"/"Enterrist" (spelling unconfirmed); Cadence and Synopsys (software-design names) are also part of his broader thematic portfolio.

quote.text: Terminal value gets harder to estimate, which makes it more difficult—companies all of a sudden can go from trading at a 30 P/E to a 20 P/E in a very short amount of time.

themes.watch: The 50-day/50% rate-of-change threshold is Visser's own proprietary signal built on his own 100-name index — it isn't a widely available or standardized indicator, and he says explicitly there's no off-the-shelf diversified benchmark that does this.

themes.status: GAVIN BAKER INTERVIEW — KEY QUOTES RELAYED
themes.title: Gavin Baker's Case: We're in an Acute Compute Shortage
themes.lead: Visser calls this the week's single most important listen — Baker's argument, in his own words, that every real-world data point on AI demand is accelerating, not decelerating.
bullets: Core claim: the AI selloff was "disconnected from the quantitative data" — Baker says he has not found a single real negative demand metric; not one instance of deceleration across GPU availability, GPU rental pricing, or DRAM spot pricing this month — "everything is actually accelerated."

Nvidia is trading at its lowest forward P/E in 10 years per Baker, who has personally bought a decent amount of Nvidia over the last three weeks; Visser agrees it's one of the safer AI names precisely because its multiple has already compressed, even though he doesn't expect it to double quickly from here.

Compute pricing is rising, not falling: the same B200 GPU cluster that rented for roughly $2-something per hour seven months ago is now expected to rent for just under $4 per GPU hour — direct evidence against the "GPUs are a depreciating bubble asset" bear case.

Key Baker quote on scarcity: "We are in acute compute shortage" — an estimated 250,000-500,000 people out of 8 billion currently use agentic AI; scaling adoption from that base to 1%, then 100 million, then 500 million implies compute demand that Baker argues will never be fully satisfied ("there will never be enough compute ever").

On hyperscalers specifically: Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon have been called an AI bubble and told their ROIC "will not come through" by bears who, per Baker/Visser, have so far been wrong — though CDS remains wider on continued heavy leverage, a separate and "justified" risk from the demand question.

Token/usage-index caveat: even the providers of the token-usage index Visser watches say a shift toward open-source usage isn't itself bearish for the market — it just reflects where the workload runs, not weakening total demand.

quote.text: We are in acute compute shortage.
quote.cite: — Gavin Baker, as relayed by Jordi Visser

themes.watch: This entire theme is Visser's summary of someone else's interview, not his own primary research — he frames it as "a must listen regardless of your views," i.e. worth checking against the original interview rather than taking as second-hand fact.

themes.status: HYPERSCALER FCF TIMELINE, GOOGLE EXITS, MEMORY BOTTLENECK
themes.title: Cracks Beneath the Boom: Hyperscaler Economics, Google's Talent Exodus, and the Memory Bottleneck
themes.lead: Even inside his own bullish framework, Visser flags three specific structural risks he thinks are underpriced.
bullets: His own post-earnings hyperscaler paper concludes he is NOT bullish on hyperscalers relative to the infrastructure trade — Goldman Sachs projects hyperscaler quarterly free cash flow as a group won't turn positive for a long time, meaning they're funding massive capex on the hope revenue eventually shows up.

His reasoning: cloud revenue alone won't be enough — hyperscalers need actual consumer/enterprise products or risk being valued like a utility or real-estate company once compute supply stops running so far ahead of demand; that's why he thinks their multiples should stay compressed and their CDS should stay wide.

Reads Jeff Dean's departure and Demis Hassabis's move to another area at Google this week as a meaningful signal of internal friction — his example is AlphaFold, released free despite Google spending heavily and taking on debt, which he thinks creates internal conflict between researchers chasing a legacy and corporate bureaucracy.

Extends this into a standing thesis: he's "negative on all public companies by the time we get to 2030" because bureaucracy will be a killer, while AI-native companies (including brand-new one-employee, million-dollar-revenue companies he's tracking) grow rapidly in parallel.

Memory bottleneck, confirmed independently: Visser wrote "AI equals memory" in June (prompting his Micron sale); on SpaceX's own earnings call this week, Elon Musk reiterated that memory — not compute — is currently the limiting factor, with memory supply growing only ~20%/year against demand growing ~200%/year or more.

His conclusion: more compute alone does not solve the AI buildout bottleneck without more memory — worth tracking as a separate trade from the GPU/compute story, and worth watching for the point where memory supply catches up to demand.

quote.text: The limiting factor currently is memory... supply is increasing by about 20% a year, the demand is increasing by 200% a year, maybe higher.
quote.cite: — Elon Musk on SpaceX's earnings call, as cited by Jordi Visser

themes.watch: The hyperscaler FCF-positive timeline is a Goldman Sachs estimate relayed secondhand, and the Musk memory-demand figures are Musk's own self-reported claim on an earnings call — both are worth checking against the primary sources before trading on them.

themes.status: FIRST COORDINATED US-JAPAN FX MOVE SINCE 1998
themes.title: Fed, Yen Intervention, and the Debasement Trade
themes.lead: A dense macro thread tying a rare currency intervention, a rate-hike standoff, and weak labor/inflation data into Visser's ongoing case for gold, silver, platinum, and Bitcoin.
bullets: The US intervened in the dollar/yen market this week — the first coordinated US-Japan FX move since 1998; Visser reads this as Treasury Secretary Bessent trying to help the Bank of Japan defend the yen without forcing Japan to sell US Treasuries to fund the defense, which would hurt the Treasury market.

Fed chair Kevin Warsh spoke last week and gave no clear guidance on rate hikes, unsettling markets; Visser flags reporting (WSJ's Nick Timiraos) that Bessent is separately leaning on the Fed to help prop up the yen — a sign, in his view, that Treasury and the Fed are coordinating more closely than usual.

As of Friday, markets priced a 45% chance of a September Fed rate hike and 63% chance of a BOJ move — Visser calls the 45% "shocking," arguing the market was "way too over their skis" a few weeks ago when multiple hikes were being priced for the rest of the year.

July was the biggest one-month rise in 30-year yields during Trump's presidency; Visser's historical pattern (repeated at "Liberation Day" and elsewhere) is that when bond yields spike this hard, the Fed/Treasury intervenes and equities then rally — "nothing stops this train," tying back to persistent 5-6% fiscal deficits and Lyn Alden's fiscal-dominance thesis.

Gold had its third-biggest week in 16 years (+7.2%), breaking back above its 50-day moving average after its third-longest stretch below that average on record (since March); platinum also broke above its 50-day, and silver closed above its 50-day for the first time — Visser holds a sizeable silver position for both AI-demand and debasement reasons.

He frames this explicitly as a "two printing presses" trade: government money-printing debases the currency wealth is measured in, while a separate "AI printing press" debases the durability of corporate equity claims — gold/silver/platinum/Bitcoin hedge the first, his AI thematic index and hedging framework address the second.

Weak labor/inflation backdrop reinforcing the debasement case: Trueflation (his preferred real-time inflation gauge) has fallen sharply for four straight weeks, diverging from official CPI; quits rate and Atlanta Fed wage growth are back to 2019 levels, average hourly earnings growth is down to 3.2%, and aggregate payrolls (hours × earnings × jobs) are at their weakest 6-month rate of change since 2012 excluding COVID, with job growth over the last 18 months coming almost entirely from healthcare.
themes.watch: Bitcoin is explicitly still in what Visser calls "a bear market until we get above there" (a level he references but doesn't fully quantify on screen) — he's constructive on the broader debasement trade but not yet calling Bitcoin's breakout confirmed; separately, the Clarity Act's odds of passing this year reportedly fell from as high as ~50% to just 17% over the prior three weeks.

names.blurb: All three broke back above their 50-day moving averages this week; Visser holds a sizeable silver position for both AI-demand and debasement reasons.

takeaways.title: Track Visser's 50-day/50%-rate-of-change signal on his AI thematic portfolio going forward — it's his stated replacement for index-put hedging, though it can't be replicated exactly without his own index.
Verify the Gavin Baker compute-pricing figures (B200 rental near $4/GPU-hour, GPU/DRAM pricing trends) against the original interview before treating them as confirmed data points.
Watch hyperscaler free-cash-flow trajectory against the Goldman Sachs timeline Visser cites — a widening capex-vs-product-revenue gap is the specific risk he's flagging, not the AI trade itself.
Follow the memory supply/demand story (Micron and peers) as a distinct trade from GPU compute — Visser's thesis is that compute alone doesn't solve the bottleneck without more memory supply.
Watch the September FOMC and BOJ decisions together, not separately — Visser's framing links the yen intervention and Fed guidance via interest-rate differentials.

If following the debasement trade (gold/silver/platinum/Bitcoin), note Visser considers Bitcoin technically still in a bear market pending an unspecified breakout level — treat it as the least-confirmed leg of that basket right now.

risks: This is one investor's personal, self-directed market commentary and trading framework (Jordi Visser and his fund's "thematic portfolio") — he discloses personal positions throughout (Palantir, silver, previously Micron), useful transparency but also a conflict worth weighing against the bullish framing.

Several of the most important figures here are second-hand: the Gavin Baker interview quotes, the Goldman Sachs hyperscaler free-cash-flow timeline, and Elon Musk's SpaceX-earnings-call memory comments are all relayed by Visser, not sourced directly — verify against the originals before treating as confirmed.

Visser's core hedging signal (50-day rate-of-change on his proprietary 100-name AI thematic index) is not a public, standardized indicator — it can't be independently reproduced without his specific portfolio construction and data feed.

A handful of individual stock names mentioned as personal holdings were not fully clear from auto-generated captions (heard as "Camores," "Enterrist") — treat those specific tickers as unconfirmed rather than accurate company names.

The transcript is auto-generated from a ~35-minute solo market-update monologue with rapid topic-switching and informal phrasing; figures (percentages, dates, price levels) have been transcribed as stated but not independently re-verified against source data or filings.

other_news.title: Personal anecdote: Visser's college-age son (not a CS major) has built an "AI chief of staff" that spins out sub-agents on its own, already used at his internship — cited as evidence agentic AI adoption is happening below the radar: "your kids have to be doing this."

Despite the Clarity Act's odds of 2026 passage reportedly falling from near 50% to 17% over three weeks, plus MicroStrategy/Michael Saylor selling more Bitcoin and a "Cold Card" hardware-wallet exploit story, Visser says Bitcoin held up fine this week regardless.

Palantir's Q2 commercial numbers: revenue growth cited at 54%/64%/149% depending on the measure, quarterly revenue up from $306M to $764M year-over-year, and 220 deals worth $1M+ (98 worth $5M+, 78 worth $10M+) closed in the quarter — Visser's core evidence for real enterprise AI adoption.

"Rise of the million-dollar, one-employee company" — Visser flags this as a fast-growing new business-formation trend he expects will gradually erode profits at larger, slower-moving public companies (Fortune 500) over time.
